You're right. I had read the last 48 hours and treated that as the whole project. I've now gone through the full handoff set: state, active tasks, the log, founder decisions 1–38, the agent matrix, the landing-page promise coverage, the design ADRs, and the contracts behind how Q's answers are shown. Here's the short version of what you've built, then A2UI.

## What Capital Q is now

Work started on 2 Sep. The branch has 5,429 commits and 239 merged PRs, and the database has 261 migrations, all applied to production.

- **Q itself:** one Q on the outside, with an answer engine, Work lanes, a team of specialist agents (research, writing, documents, outreach, scheduling) and standing instructions underneath. It sits behind the Context Firewall and a single model gateway, and consequential actions go Prepare → Recommend → your approval → Execute.
- **Investor side:**
  - mandate onboarding;
  - Discover, the video feed with a ranked mandate fit;
  - company profiles as decision briefs;
  - an evidence-graded data room;
  - compare tables;
  - top-N ranking;
  - drafting emails and replies, with approval cards.
- **Founder side:**
  - a conversational onboarding interview with deck reading and confirmation;
  - readiness, and InvestIQ as FDN's method (running in shadow mode only);
  - "which investors fit me", with fit levels set by code only;
  - investor rehearsals and GateQ.
- **Q Pitch / Q Story:**
  - the 12-minute investor script;
  - Tavus presenters, also in Google Meet;
  - GPT-Live voice;
  - the Qatar Five prepared entities;
  - Q Daily.
- **Organisation roles,** with your rule that admins never see a member's private Q content.
- **Design:** the black-and-gold brand, a Stage and Board that has since become a chat thread by default, Light · Device · Dark switching, and the Q Dock.
- **The arc:** Claude led until 11 Oct, Codex led after that, then Claude coordinated again from 20 Oct. Along the way you hit Railway outages, revoked provider keys, and running out of web-search providers until only Serper was left. QA climbed from 89.6% to 93.75% to 99.0%.

## A2UI: you already built the core of it

I cloned Google's repo and read the spec. It's the v0.9.1 stable family, with a v1.0 release candidate. The idea is that an agent sends JSON describing UI, and the app draws it with its own pre-approved components ("safe like data, expressive like code"). It defines four messages that build a screen area and update it piece by piece (`createSurface`, `updateComponents`, `updateDataModel`, `deleteSurface`), plus an `action` event when the user clicks something.

Capital Q has had the same idea since the design phase:

- **A fixed set of building blocks.** Every Q answer is built from 22 typed blocks that no model can add to: comparison, evidence, finding, uncertainty, action proposal, table, chart, timeline, picture, work in progress and others (`packages/contracts/src/q/result-block.ts`).
- **Each block is checked on its own,** so one bad block is dropped without losing the rest of the answer.
- **The rule is written down.** ADR 0017 says answers use fixed components chosen by Q, never model-generated code. Your design research doc even cites Gemini's generative UI as the inspiration, and drew this conclusion from it.
- **Screens fill in progressively.** Cards go up while Q is still talking and fill in when the blocks land, and 21 kinds of screen action cover navigating, opening pages and so on.

## Why adopting A2UI as the core would be a step backwards

1. **Its blocks are layout pieces, ours carry meaning.** A2UI's components are Text, Row, Column, Card, Button and TextField. Ours are things like COMPARISON and EVIDENCE, which carry truth class, evidence status and the gold-badge rule. If Q built answers out of Rows and Text, a model could make a guess look like a verified fact, and "unknown stays unknown" would no longer be enforced by the screen.
2. **It sends data, we send references.** A2UI puts the actual data into the app. Q's blocks deliberately carry only IDs, which the app looks up under the viewer's own permissions. Switching would make every Q answer a second, unchecked copy of company records. That is a Context Firewall problem.
3. **Its actions are a generic catch-all.** A clickable component can send any action name with free-form data. That runs against your "no generic action endpoint" rule, idempotency keys, and approval tied to the exact proposal.
4. **It's slower.** Since v0.9, the model writes the UI JSON itself. Output length is exactly what you've been cutting: the reader writing only the fields that apply saved 0.85 s per turn, and the compare writer was narrowed for the same reason. Your tables are built by code from checked reads, with no model in the way.
5. **It's not mature, and it doesn't fit our stack.** The project calls itself an "early stage public preview", its React renderer is at 0.14, it needs zod 3 while we use zod 4.5.4, and it assumes Google's agent transports instead of our own stream.

## What's worth borrowing

- **Filling in parts of a block.** A2UI can update one piece of a component in place. Applied to the compare table, cells would fill as each read lands, rather than the table waiting for the whole block. That helps the "first visible change" score and the ~7 s before Q answers.
- **Telling the model exactly what was wrong.** A2UI has a standard error format so the model can retry with precise feedback. The 43 s readiness answer was mostly whole-answer rewrites; targeted feedback would make those cheaper.
- **Inputs inside answers.** A2UI lets an answer carry choices and fields that bind to values. Clarification questions and onboarding confirmations could carry tap-to-answer choices in the same way.
- **Later, if Q has to show up inside other people's agent tools:** a translator at the edge that turns Q's blocks into a Capital Q catalog for those tools. Our blocks stay the source of truth. Not now.

My call: don't adopt A2UI. Your design is already stricter where it matters. The first item is the one worth building, but after the remaining database calls, which are still #1 on the handover list. Either way, nothing here changes a locked decision. I haven't changed any code; I only checked out `speed/q-oct20` locally to read it.

Sources:
- [google/A2UI on GitHub](https://github.com/google/A2UI)
- [a2ui.org](https://a2ui.org/)
- [CopilotKit: Google's A2UI spec](https://www.copilotkit.ai/blog/build-with-googles-new-a2ui-spec-agent-user-interfaces-with-a2ui-ag-ui)
- [jimmysong.io A2UI overview](https://jimmysong.io/ai/a2ui)

### Claude — 2026-10-27 20:38 UTC

Yes, it makes sense. It's a better design than the one we have, and you should have had it weeks ago. I searched the handoff files and **your suggestion isn't recorded anywhere**. That's part of why we keep going in circles: each new session inherits the old per-turn design and patches it again. I'll write it into `DECISIONS.md` so it sticks.

**Why the current design keeps breaking**

Today every single thing you say goes through a chain:
1. voice model
2. hand-off to the interviewer
3. a model reads the turn
4. a save check
5. a database write
6. a reply

That's up to 4 model calls and 2–9 s per turn. Today's session failed at two links in that chain: the voice line was refused after your firm was created, and your Series A answer was rejected by the "starts with What" rule. Every fix so far has patched one link, and the next one breaks. More patches won't settle it.

**Your design**

1. **Connect, and Q introduces itself straight away.** It says who it is, what it's going to do and roughly how long it takes. Meanwhile the web search on you runs in the background, and if it finds something solid, Q uses it.
2. **Q just talks with you.** The voice model is given the list of things it needs: investor type, stages, sectors, countries, cheque size and so on. It has the whole conversation in its own memory, so it knows what's been answered and won't re-ask. Nothing is saved per turn, so there's nothing to fail per turn. Each reply is roughly 1 s instead of 2–9 s.
3. **The transcript is saved as you go,** tied to *you*, not your organisation. A dropped call loses nothing.
4. **When you finish, one background step reads the whole transcript.** It pulls out each answer and shows them on one confirmation card: "Here's your mandate: accelerator, pre-seed to Series A…". You tap to confirm or fix anything, then it saves. That fits the existing rule that facts Q extracts must be confirmed before they count.
5. **It's fast.** That one extraction call takes about 3–8 s, once, instead of 4 model calls on every turn. And because it reads the whole conversation, "What do you mean… I mainly do Series A" is understood correctly, with no keyword rules.

**What we keep:** the confirmation card ("keep all N") already exists for document readings, the transcript table exists, and the web research on you already runs in parallel. This mostly removes machinery rather than adding it.

**Two things to accept:**
- Nothing is saved until the end. If you leave halfway, the transcript is still there and extraction runs on whatever you said.
- The voice model alone decides which question to ask next. The list keeps it on track, and the extraction catches anything that was skipped.

So yes: I'll stop patching the old per-turn flow. Say go and I'll build this for investor and founder onboarding:
- test it locally with no paid calls;
- deploy once;
- then do one short live voice check with you.

The voice line stayed tied to your old account context, so from 20:22:20 on every call from it was refused. Q was cut off from everything that saves answers and carried on alone.
- **Your Series A answer rejected.** Speech-to-text gave it as one run-on sentence starting "What do you mean…". A keyword rule treated any sentence starting with "What" as a question.
- **A bug found while building the fix.** For weeks, live calls stored almost nothing the person said (for example, 1 of your lines against 51 of Q's). A missing field in the web relay silently rejected exactly the batches that carried your words.

**What I built, for both investor and founder:**
- **Real introduction.** Q says who it is, what you'll do together and why, roughly how long, that you can stop any time, and that the form is there if you'd rather type. Then it asks a plain first question. It's built by code, so it's instant, and web research on you starts at the same moment.
- **A conversation, not a form.** Q works from the setup's checklist in its own words, one thing at a time, grouping related questions and saying lightly when something is optional. It asks you to spell a website if unsure, and every step now has a plain spoken question.
- **Saving in the background.** The conversation is saved to your onboarding as it happens. About 2.5 seconds after each thing you say, and again when you leave, a background step reads the whole conversation and saves what you said. Your latest answer wins and the old one is kept as history. It runs on the server, so closing the tab loses nothing, and next time Q picks up where you stopped.
- **Read-back from the database.** When you ask what Q has, Q reads it back from what's actually saved and asks what's missing. A spoken "yes, let's finish" completes the setup.
- **"Continue later"** is now in voice, not just the form.
- **Uploads.** A document card shows a skeleton while Q reads it. What Q finds, and what web research finds, goes into the live conversation so it doesn't ask again.
- **Fixes.** Voice now follows you into your new organisation (and still never between two organisations), the keyword rule is gone, and the relay passes your words through.
- **Rollback.** Setting `CQ_ONBOARDING_VOICE_CONVERSATION=off` on q-api brings the old guided interview back.

**Tests:** q-api 2,592 pass, web 3,505 pass, packages 2,459 pass, and there are 0 type errors. New tests reuse your exact sentences and cover a brand-new account whose organisation is created during the call.

**Still unproven:**
- **How the live voice model follows the new instructions, and how well the transcript reader works on a real model.** That can only be checked with a real call; every test uses fakes and no provider was called.
- **A restart of q-api during a call still drops that call,** as before. What was already saved stays.

**For your boss:** be honest that this is built and tested in code but not yet tried live. The earlier "onboarding 100%" covered typed onboarding on existing accounts, never voice or a new client. I've recorded that, the conversation-first approach and the no-keyword rule as owner decisions 39–41 in `docs/ai-handoff/DECISIONS.md`, and written the full state to `docs/ai-handoff/HANDOFF-2026-10-27.md`.

**Next:** once CI is green I'll deploy all four services, check they're live, and then it's ready for one short voice test with a fresh investor account. Please also rotate the Railway and Supabase tokens you pasted in chat.

## Is Capital Q ready to onboard startups?

**Yes for a controlled pilot. Not yet for an open launch.** I'd start with 10–50 hand-picked startups and investors you can talk to directly.

**Why the pilot is fine:**
- The foundations are unusually strong for five weeks of work:
  - tenant isolation and the Context Firewall;
  - answers that cite their evidence;
  - every action approved by a person first;
  - one record per company–investor relationship;
  - about 9,000 automated tests.
- Typed onboarding scored 99% on QA.
- Voice onboarding now saves what people say reliably, which I checked on production.

**What I'd fix before going wider, in order of risk:**

1. **Real customer data is labelled as demo data.** Every production model call I read, including last night's onboarding session, carried `dataPosture: "SYNTHETIC_DEMO"`. Before real founders upload real financials:
   - mark their data as real customer data, so the routing rules for private data apply;
   - confirm the AI providers' data-retention terms;
   - publish a privacy policy and get users' consent.

   This is the one I'd treat as a must.
2. **Voice hasn't been tried on a real device since the rebuild.** That's your 2-minute test. Founder onboarding in the new mode hasn't been run live at all; I only tested investor. Run one founder through with a real deck.
3. **Fragile pieces:**
   - Web search depends on one provider (Serper). The other three are out of credit or blocked.
   - Live calls are held in one server's memory, so every deploy drops any call in progress.
   - Railway's builder failed several times this week.
   - The tokens pasted in chat still need rotating.
4. **Some of what Q's intelligence promises is unproven.**
   - **Strong:**
     - finding and comparing companies against a mandate (code-computed and explainable);
     - answering questions from the record with sources;
     - drafting messages that a person approves.
   - **Not yet proven:**
     - InvestIQ scoring runs only in the background and hasn't been calibrated on real companies;
     - the agents that do research and documents can only handle narrow tasks so far, not open-ended due diligence;
     - deck-reading quality on messy real decks.

   The landing page says more than has been verified. The promise-coverage file marks most claims as "the feature exists", with few verified live.
5. **It won't scale yet.** Ranking one investor's top five still takes about 360 database queries; a well-built system needs 10–50. Fine for a pilot, but not for thousands of users.

## What would 1 million users cost?

These are rough figures from the measured per-call costs above and list prices, which I haven't checked against your contracts. The answer depends mostly on how much video and voice people use.

**Onboarding everyone (one-time):**

| | Per user | 1M users |
|---|---|---|
| Typed onboarding (~15 Q turns) | ~$0.15 | ~$150k |
| Voice onboarding (~5 min live voice plus readings) | ~$0.35–0.60 | ~$350–600k |
| Web research and deck reading | ~$0.01–0.05 | ~$10–50k |

Realistic mix: **about $250k–500k**. You also couldn't onboard a million people in one day: the AI providers' rate limits and the database would stop you first.

**Monthly running costs**, assuming 30% of users active each month:

| Item | Assumption | Per month |
|---|---|---|
| Q text answers | 10 per active user | ~$30k |
| Live voice | 10% of users, 10 min each | ~$60k |
| AI video presenters (rehearsals, GateQ interviews) | 5% of users, 10 min each | **~$150–200k**, the biggest risk; keep the existing caps |
| Pitch video storage and playback | | ~$10–20k |
| Web search, emails, embeddings | | ~$5k |
| Database and hosting at that scale | needs a move off the current setup | ~$15–40k |

Total: **about $270k–350k a month**, or roughly **$0.30–1.20 per active user per month**. Video and voice are about 80% of the bill. Subscriptions or usage caps on them decide whether the business works.

**Training your own model:**
- **Building a model from scratch:** tens of millions of dollars, and not worth it. Your edge is your data and your rules, not raw model power.
- **Fine-tuning small open models on your own logs (sensible):**
  - **What:** the turn reader, the onboarding extraction and the routing classifiers. These make thousands of calls a day.
  - **One-time cost:** about $2k–20k per training round on rented GPUs.
  - **Hosting:** about $10k–40k a month for dedicated GPUs, roughly 2–8 H100s at $2–4/hour.
  - **Payoff:** likely 30–60% cheaper per call on those readers, and faster, because the readers add about 3.5 s before Q starts answering.
  - **Not before you have volume:** at today's ~$23 a week, it's far cheaper to keep paying the providers.

**My recommendation:** run the pilot now, after fixing item 1 and doing your voice test. Use the pilot to measure real usage per user, especially video and voice minutes, before committing to pricing or training your own model. If it would help with your boss, I can turn this into a one-page readiness and cost brief.

Here's the answer to your funding question, then I'm starting on the three jobs.

## What to ask investors for, over 24 months

These are planning figures, not supplier quotes. The ask splits into four parts.

**1. Q's own model**, fine-tuning open-weight models (LoRA) on your own data, retrained regularly as data grows:

| Item | 24 months |
|---|---|
| Licensed data: deal, company and market data (e.g. Crunchbase/PitchBook-type, Africa- and Gulf-focused datasets) | $150k–300k |
| Data pipeline: storage, cleaning, labelling by analysts (tens of thousands of checked examples) | $60k–150k |
| Training compute: monthly retraining runs on rented GPUs, more often when there's new data | $150k–350k |
| Evaluation and safety testing (each new version has to beat the last before it ships) | $40k–80k |
| Serving the fine-tuned models: start on pay-per-use hosts, move to dedicated GPUs as volume grows | $150k–500k |
| ML team: 2 ML engineers and 1 data engineer | $450k–900k |
| **Subtotal** | **≈ $1.0M–2.3M** |

**2. Running Capital Q**, assuming it grows to tens of thousands of active users in year 1 and a few hundred thousand in year 2 (not 1M on day one):

| Item | 24 months |
|---|---|
| AI providers: text, voice, video presenters, search | $1.0M–2.3M (video and voice are ~80% of it; usage caps matter) |
| Hosting, database, video delivery, monitoring | $300k–600k |
| Security audit (e.g. SOC 2), penetration tests, data-protection compliance (NDPR, GDPR, Gulf PDPL), data stored locally where required | $150k–350k |
| **Subtotal** | **≈ $1.5M–3.3M** |

**3. Team** beyond the ML hires (product, engineering, design, analyst support for founders): 6–10 people, **≈ $1.2M–3.0M**.

**4. Go-to-market and legal** (sales in Nigeria and the Gulf, partnerships, entity setup): **≈ $0.5M–1.5M**.

**The ask:**
- **Lean: about $3.5M.** Fine-tuned readers and Q's analyst voice, a careful launch, a small team.

### Claude — 2026-10-28 08:24 UTC

I've kept your existing setup: test accounts are demo, and anyone signing up normally is a real customer. Nothing got stricter, and real people can onboard right now. The code that makes this hold everywhere is in CI and not deployed yet. I'll check CI at about 08:49 UTC and deploy if it's green.

**How the two are told apart:** a hidden `synthetic` flag on the account, which only the server can set; a user can't add it. All your seeded accounts and your own `adedaniel…+cq-…` aliases carry it. Real signups (Tiara, David Nwankwo, Fortune, the Zino Aviation account and so on) don't. I went with the flag rather than "Gmail vs test email" because your demo aliases are Gmail addresses too.

**What the live database shows:**
- **Verification badges were already right.** "Demo verified (synthetic)" only goes to flagged accounts. None of the 40 real accounts has one; all 977 demo badges belong to the demo world.
- **The gap was which AI provider handles a request.** The demo setting applied to every request, so if OpenAI failed, a real person's data could fall back to Gemini's free tier. Google's terms there allow training on the data.

**What I changed:**
1. **Model routing.** Demo treatment now applies only when the person and their organisation are flagged demo. If an organisation has even one real member, it counts as real. If the check fails, the request is treated as real. This covers Q, the background workers and GateQ.
2. **Voice.** It used to depend on the demo setting, so it would have refused real people once the demo treatment no longer applied to them. It now uses OpenAI's own approval level, so voice works for real people too.

On the live data, a seeded demo account comes out as demo and Tiara comes out as real. The 21 new tests and both typechecks pass.

**Why nothing gets stricter:** over the last 7 days every successful AI call already went to OpenAI, and all 238 Gemini calls failed anyway. Q never sends anything above OpenAI's approval level: nobody can see private financials, and highly confidential documents never go to an AI provider.

**One side effect:** test accounts I made through the normal sign-up page (like the Kemi investor) aren't flagged, so they now count as real. They still work normally.

When you're ready for a separate production database and subdomain, moving a real person or organisation across is a per-tenant export. I've recorded this as decision 42 in the handoff docs.

The deck-reading and due-diligence fixes are still running in the background, each on its own branch. I'll report back when they finish.

## Answers for your boss

**1. Can founders start onboarding now, with Q helping on their data room and questions? Yes, with caveats.**
- **What works today:**
  - A founder signs up, uploads their deck and documents, and Q reads them and fills in the company profile.
  - Q asks only for what's missing.
  - Founders can ask Q about their own company and their documents.
  - They can manage the data room and deck, run rehearsals, and see their readiness.
  - The investor side has Discover and the swipe feed.
  - Real signups are now kept separate from the demo data.
- **Caveat 1, messy decks:** scanned or image-only decks get little or nothing read today, and long decks are only partly read. A fix is in progress.
- **Caveat 2, due diligence:** "Do due diligence and write a memo" currently gives a thin, record-only memo. A fix is in progress.
- **Caveat 3, voice:** voice onboarding has been checked on the server, but not yet on a real phone.

**Link to share:** https://capital-qweb-production.up.railway.app/auth/sign-up
- Founders should use their real email.
- For a meeting, the safest promise is "upload your deck and documents, and Q helps you complete your profile and data room." That's the strong part today.

**2. What does $100K buy, and how many users can it carry?** These are rough estimates, not quotes.
- **Running costs are small.** Last week's measured AI cost was about $0.02 per Q answer and $0.02 per voice call. An active founder costs a few dollars a month in AI. Hosting plus database runs a few hundred to about $2,000 a month as usage grows.
- **The current system carries roughly a few thousand active users.** Beyond that, scaling work is needed: a heavy discovery ranking path, and voice calls held in one server's memory.
- **$100K would cover about 12 months of:**
  - running costs for roughly 2,000–5,000 active users;

### Claude — 2026-10-28 09:04 UTC

You were right. The earlier figure was too optimistic. Here it is redone, built from measured per-unit costs and stated usage assumptions rather than last week's handful of testers.

**What each thing costs.** Measured means taken from production over the last 14 days or set in the code; estimated means a vendor list price I haven't checked against an invoice.

| What a user does | Cost per unit | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Q answer, typed (3–4 model calls) | $0.006 average, $0.013 for the costliest 10% | measured |
| Q's background work (classifying, extracting, translating) | adds about 80% on top of answers, so about $0.011 per answer in total | measured |
| Voice call with Q | $0.05 per minute | rate in the code |
| Video with a Tavus presenter (GateQ, rehearsals, meetings) | **$0.36 per minute** | measured |
| Generated image (decks, documents) | $0.04 each | measured |
| Web search / reading a web page | about $1 / $1.50 per 1,000 | estimated |
| Reading scanned deck pages (new) | about $0.002–0.005 per page | estimated |
| Database and file storage | 390 MB and 223 MB for 1,329 accounts, so negligible | measured |

**What one active user costs per month**

| User | What they do in a month | Cost per month |
|---|---|---|
| Light founder | about 60 Q answers, 5 voice minutes, no video | $1–2 |
| Typical founder | about 300 Q answers (15 a workday), 30 voice minutes, 2 rehearsals (6 video minutes), about 10 document readings or drafts, about 100 searches | **about $8** |
| Heavy founder | about 1,000 answers, 2 hours of voice, the full video allowance (5 sessions a week, 60 minutes) | **about $40**, of which $22 is video |
| Typical investor | swiping costs no AI; about 150 Q answers, 10 voice minutes, a few diligence memos | $3–5 |

With a realistic mix and video capped at 15 minutes a month, that averages **about $8 per active user per month**. Video is the biggest risk: without a cap, a heavy user can cost $40.

**Infrastructure** (for a separate production setup):
- About $800 a month at around 500 active users.
- About $2,000 a month at around 2,000.
- About $4,000 a month at around 5,000.
- It covers the database (with backups and later a read replica), the four servers (each running in two copies), voice-session storage, monitoring, email and video streaming.
- The OpenAI account's rate limits and the Tavus plan's concurrent-session limit will also need raising as numbers grow.

**What $100K buys, over 12 months:**
- **Hardening, about $20–30K one-off:**
  - a production database and domain, plus moving real customers across;
  - fixing the two scaling bottlenecks: a ranking takes about 360 database round trips, and voice calls are held in one server's memory;
  - load testing and a security review.
- **Running, the remaining $70–80K:**
  - about $12–24K for infrastructure;
  - $50–65K for usage, which at about $8 per active user carries **about 500–700 active users on average for a year**, or about 1,000–1,500 for six months;
  - registered users who aren't active cost almost nothing.
- **Cost levers, which roughly double that:**
  - cap or charge for video;
  - trim Q's 33,000-token context per answer (58% of it is already cached);
  - run background work on cheaper models;
  - cap voice minutes.
  - Together they bring it to about $4 per active user, or **about 1,200–1,500 active users for a year**.
- **Today, without the hardening work,** the system realistically handles a few hundred users at the same time.

These figures don't include anyone's salary. The usage numbers in the per-user table are assumptions; I can put them in a spreadsheet so your boss can change them himself.

**Living on the Q page:** documents, drafts, approval cards, "who's interested in me", accepting interest by voice or card, relationship replies, itinerary, profile updates and questions about specific investors are all being checked now, against the code with file references, for both founders and investors. You'll get a clear yes/partial/no table with the gaps a founder would hit in their first week, not my memory of what Q once did. After that, I'll run the most important ones live as a test founder on production.

**Item 12 — things a person needs that Q cannot do on the Q page:**
- No schedule or calendar view anywhere in the app.
- Recording a pitch and rehearsals only work by going to their pages (`NEW_PITCH`, `REHEARSALS`).
- Q cannot send files or voice notes in a chat.
- Founder-uploaded files cannot be edited.
- Billing and plan pages are only reachable by navigation.

**Behind a flag, gated, or account-dependent:**
- Live and full-duplex voice are off unless `CQ_VOICE_LIVE` is "on" (plus a user allow-list, `CQ_VOICE_LIVE_USERS`) or `CQ_VOICE_REALTIME` is "on" (`voice/live/config.ts:100-108`, `voice/duplex/config.ts:91`).
- Q acting on standing instructions by itself needs `CQ_INSTRUCTIONS_AUTO=on` (`main.ts:2531`).
- How documents get built depends on `CQ_DOCUMENT_PIPELINE` (`main.ts:4256-4262`).
- Public-web research only exists when a research provider is set up, and it uses up the plan's research allowance (`default-tools.ts:92-127`).
- Errands and delegated jobs are checked against the billing plan.
- Fictional/demo accounts skip investor research (`voice/investor-research.ts:468-476`).
- Email and calendar features need Google connected.

**Top gaps, most likely first in a founder's first accelerator week:**
1. **"What's on today?"** Q answers only in text. There is no schedule card, no schedule page to open, and no calendar page (#8).
2. **Editing a reply before it goes.** Chat replies to investors can't be edited on the card, only re-asked through "Change it" (`q-now.tsx:115-139` special-cases email only) (#2, #5).
3. **Email needs Gmail first.** Without a connected Gmail, drafting an email to an investor stalls (#2).
4. **No investor-update document type** for the common monthly update (#2).
5. **Uploaded deck or data-room files can't be edited**, only viewed, downloaded, renamed or archived (#1).
6. **Investor interest has no dedicated list card.** It arrives as text; deciding works on the approval card, or Q opens the interest page and the person leaves the Q page (#4).
7. **Chat is text-only.** Q cannot send files or voice notes in a relationship chat (#5).
8. **Navigation leaves the Q page.** Any page Q opens takes the person away. Only cards from `show` stay on the page (#10).
9. **Voice depends on deployment flags.** Live and duplex voice are off unless enabled, so the voice experience depends on how the deployment is set up.</result>

### Claude — 2026-10-28 09:25 UTC

The deck-reading fix is ready on its own branch (`fix/deck-reading`, commit `78ab9587c`): tested locally, not merged or deployed, no migration. What it changes, in plain terms:

- **The whole deck is read, not the first 12 chunks.** Passages are sampled evenly across every page, first and last always included, so traction and the ask at the end of a 60-slide deck are seen.
- **PDF layout is read properly.** Columns and table cells no longer get scrambled; right-to-left text is handled; page markers are exact.
- **Money is read as money.** ₦, KSh, R, $, £, €, AED, INR; "1,5 M€", "1 500 000", "1.500.000", Arabic digits, lakh/crore. The deck's own currency is kept. If it differs from what the founder chose, Q raises it as a question instead of quietly relabelling the amount.
- **Scanned and image-only pages are transcribed** by a vision model through the gateway, capped at 30 pages and $0.60 per document, respecting the document's confidentiality level. If that isn't available, the founder is told: "N pages were images I couldn't read." PNG and JPEG uploads are now accepted instead of rejected.
- **PowerPoint speaker notes and chart data** are read. pdf.js now has its font maps, so CID and Arabic fonts no longer come out empty.
- **Contradictions between slides of the same deck** are flagged, non-English decks keep the original wording with an English gloss, and truncation is reported to the founder.

All gates pass: 0 type errors, about 7,900 tests, lint and formatting clean. A synthetic 60-page messy deck is tested end to end. The main limits: no eval against a real deck yet, and typed interview answers like "₦18m" are still stored under the chosen currency.

Both fixes are now ready to merge: deck reading and due diligence. I'll give each a quick review before merging, especially the diligence claims matcher, which I want to check against your no-pattern rule. Then I'll run CI and deploy, after the live-run reports, which come first.

## Root causes (from production q-api logs, window 10:17–10:45 UTC)

**D1 — investor answers not saved.** Log `10:39:19.559 interview q run traced` (req_4566b7fa): the reading stated all 10 steps and the model recorded them, but `record_answers:I0.investor_type … COMMITTED` saved `{"type":"TEXT","text":"I'm an angel, also run a small syndicate…"}` (DB confirms), and website/status/stages/currency/cheque_min/max/geography/sectors were `HELD_FOR_RETRY: Kept, and saved automatically as soon as their firm … is set up`. `bootstrapInvestor` (packages/investor-onboarding/src/integration/write-targets.ts:753) needs the type as an option key, so no firm existed (`onboarding.sessions.tenant_id` null) and every later write was refused `onboarding_context_required`; the correction (`10:39:28 correct_answer:I2.cheque_min … HELD_FOR_RETRY`) and "6 deals" (`10:40:37 I2.investment_role HELD`) waited on the same thing, and the held replay hit HTTP_500 (`pending_writes.last_error`). The port's single-select fallback "none of the options → their words as TEXT" (onboarding-port.ts) caused it. Fix: `OPTION_ONLY_STEPS` (I0.investor_type) is never saved as text; it is handed back `UNMATCHED` with the options and the model records `angel` on the next round (`apps/q-api/src/voice/onboarding-port.ts:~96, ~1133, ~1329, ~1385`). The founder path never hits this because the company bootstraps from a text name.

**D3 — "that's all for now" paused and went Home.** `10:40:50 traced … asking null, finishing false`; `navigate: "HOME"` came from `pausing = authority.pausing || (!canComplete &amp;&amp; (finishing || asksToLeave(utterance)))` — `asksToLeave` was a regex list (onboarding-flow.ts `LEAVING`, a DECISIONS 40 violation) and pausing → HOME. Fix: `LEAVING`/`asksToLeave` deleted; on the typed channel a pausing reading is finishing (`stoppingIsFinishing`, interview-agent.ts:~480); after the round code calls `port.finish()` (confirms review steps on their word, completes when essentials met) and writes the reply itself: done line, or "Before I can finish, I still need N things: … &lt;first question&gt;" with `asking` set (`finishingLine`, onboarding-flow.ts:~455; agent ~2745). HOME navigation only remains for the spoken guided interview's pause. The "I haven't saved that yet" prefix is now only used when the reading stated something unsaved (agent ~2810).

**D4 — founder figures.** Note "KSh 2.; 1m" from `fieldClausesOf` splitting on `.` (onboarding-port.ts:~3800): decimals between digits are now protected. "$2.1 million": `recordedCurrency` took the journey's first `.currency` step (F6 raise USD); it now prefers the money step's own phase (F5.fin_currency = KES) (`interview-steps.ts:481`, port `spoken()`). "61 (gross margin)" → range steps read with their unit ("61%"), and a note receipt says "growth kept in your notes" instead of echoing the quote (quick-acknowledgement.ts:173). "400k" not saved that turn: STEP_NOT_ELIGIBLE because F6.raising was later in the same batch; the batch now replays held step-waiting writes once after it commits (port `waitingOnStep`, ~2555–2600).

**D5 — re-asking.** Company name: `firstOpening` never settled known answers (only `resumeOpening` did); it now records the journey choice and the sign-up organisation name before choosing the first question (onboarding-conductor.ts:~1034). Stages: follows from D1. Skipped strict/balanced: `10:40:23 traced … declined: []` — DELEGATION_READER v2–v5 said "Required steps are never declined", so the model set aside the wrong step (I0.website, REJECTED) and the question returned. New prompt `DELEGATION_READER` v6 (v5 DEPRECATED, lock regenerated) reads the decline; the agent remembers declined required steps per session (`declinedForNow`), the flow treats them as set aside, the model is told, and finishing lists them.

[SendMessage → Keep pausing = leave; finishing = finish]
One correction before this merges (owner rule 2026-10-28, DECISIONS/HANDOFF-2026-10-27: "continue later" takes the person INTO the app, with the gentle reminders bringing them back). Do not collapse pausing into finishing on the typed channel. Keep the two readings the reader already distinguishes by meaning:
- pausing ("I'll continue this later", "not now", "let me come back to this") → save everything heard (the reading), reply with one short line saying what is saved and what is still open, then LEAVE: navigate to Discover for an investor, Home for a founder (the same destinations as the Continue later button / continueLaterDestination). Never complete the session on a pause, never ask the next question.
- finishing ("that's all", "I'm done", "finish", "that's everything") → port.finish(): complete when essentials are met, else the "Before I can finish, I still need N things: … <first question>" line, as you built.
Revert `stoppingIsFinishing` for the pausing case; keep your finishingLine for finishing; keep the HOME/Discover navigation for pausing on the typed channel (it was the investor "that's all" going Home by itself that was wrong — because "that's all" is finishing, not pausing). ## 1. Tiara / The Vaultlyne voice onboarding (session `193cc214`, completed 13:56:41)

**(a) Cheque saved as raw transcript text.**
- **What happened:** she said "I do the dollars and Um, pounds", so the reader returned two options (USD and GBP). The currency question only allows one answer, and the port turns more than one choice into her own words. Those words are the transcript itself. The current saved answer is that text; an earlier save had stored "Yeah, just those two".
- **Code:** `onboarding-port.ts:1343-1350` and `:1366-1381` (`ownWordsFor` at `:1143`). The profile page then upper-cases any text currency and puts it in front of the amount (`apps/web/.../profile-answers.ts:245-266`).
- **Worse than the display:** the mandate gets cheque amounts only from a proper currency choice (`write-targets.ts:372-391`). Her mandate row (`d0e986e9`) has no currency and no minimum or maximum cheque, so matching never sees her cheque sizes.
- **Fix:** never save a money currency as free text. Either allow more than one currency, or keep the first and ask about the other.

**(b) Optional questions never asked.**
- **Why Q stopped:** only 10 steps are required. Once those were in, the read-back says "Everything needed is in" and tells the voice to wrap up (`onboarding-conversation.ts:813` and `:822`). The live prompt also tells it to finish once the essentials are covered (`live/prompt.ts:58`). The checklist does list the optional steps, but nothing tells the voice to ask them. Sectors and exclusions were only covered because she pushed for them.
- **Lead/follow:** Q asked it at 13:33:39 and the line ended on idle before she answered. On resume, the opening jumps to the next required step (`:705-708`), so it was never asked again.
- **Website, country and headline** aren't steps in the investor journey at all, so they can only ever show "Not added".
- **Also found:** her hard exclusions ended up as only "adult content". The 13:56:23 save replaced crypto and gambling, and religion survives only as a note on the sectors to avoid.
- **Fix:** tell the voice, in the read-back and the setup prompt, to offer the optional topics in groups before finishing. On resume, continue in setup order instead of jumping to the next required step.

**(c) No move to Discover.**
- **What happened:** when she asked to finish, the session completed, but the finish reply has no "leave" flag (`onboarding-conversation.ts:562`). Only the "stop for now" path sets it (`:543-547`), and the browser navigates only when that flag is set (`live-call.ts:553`). When she then asked to go to Discover, Q said "That's coming up on your screen now", but nothing moved and the line ended idle at 13:59:19.
- **Fix:** return the leave flag on completion, and on any later request once the session is complete.

**(d) The upload.** It wasn't during onboarding. She uploaded the 28-page PDF at 14:24:55 on the Q page, during a different call, and it was extracted fine.
- **Not spoken:** the "Summarise it" request went out as a written turn that bypasses the open voice line (`q-conversation.tsx:769-773`). The text summary was never spoken, and when she asked about the document the voice replied "Tell me which one you're looking at".
- **Not fully read:** only about 8,000 characters of the document go into the prompt (`attached-document-fact.ts:23`). Q presented its key points as a summary of the whole document, then admitted it had only seen the opening pages.
- **Fix:** send it into the line when a call is open, and have Q say when a summary is partial.

## 2. Nixo founder: the document job (run `9000575e`, job `9e52faf7`)
- **Timeline:** the request came in at 14:04:15. The only stage the screen ever got was "Pulling it together"; two classification calls timed out along the way. At 14:04:40 Q said it had started.
  - Research ran from 14:04:41 to 14:05:21 (8 searches, 30 sources).
  - Three drafts were written and reviewed; the final review still failed with 12 open issues.
  - The analysis was filed and the "is ready" message posted at 14:08:05. Total time was about 3 minutes 25 seconds.
- **Why it wasn't announced:**
  - The voice line ended on idle at 14:06:59, before the document existed.
  - The browser stopped re-reading the conversation at 14:04:58.
  - The progress card only started checking the job at 14:07:49. When it saw "done" it only re-read the conversation; it never opens the document (`work-live.tsx:187-191`, `q-session.tsx:399-403`).
  - The "ready" pop-up is suppressed when the document is already on screen, and it disappears after 12 seconds anyway.
  - She opened the document herself at 14:08:59.
- **Fix:** open the delivered document from the "work settled" handler in `q-session.tsx`. Don't let the call idle out while promised work is running, or push a "ready" note into the line from `delivery.ts` (lines 261-330).

## 3. TensorGate founder: "can't" (run `8b649d10`, 14:10:50)
- **Request:** "Can you make it into a plan and then go ahead and execute that plan for me." **Reply:** "I couldn't turn that into a plan I can carry out, so nothing has started…"
- **Not a permission refusal:** the firewall authorised the turn with no denials.
- **What happened:** the planner returned an empty plan (log line at `jobs.ts:1196`, "steps:0"). An empty plan is reported as "not planned" (`job-actions.ts:797-799`).
- **Root cause:** the job's goal is built from her own words only (`answer.ts:5882-5891`, `team-job.ts:243-254`), by design. So "that plan" reached the planner without the gaps list Q had just given.
- **Second problem:** the reply text asks for "questions for the founder", which is investor wording shown to a founder.
- **Fix:** when the request points at Q's last answer, pass that answer to the planner as context (marked as Q's inference, not as the goal). Make the "not planned" text match the user's role.</result>

**Design choice:** a new `SPREADSHEET` artifact type whose stored content carries a typed `workbook` alongside the usual sections, the same way a deck carries `content.deck`.
- **No migration needed.** The artifact type column is checked by a regex, not an enum.
- **Downloads are .xlsx and .csv, not PDF.** A PDF would only show the short summary, not the data.

**What changed:**
- **Contract** (`packages/contracts/src/q/spreadsheet.ts`, new):
  - Columns are text, number, money, percent, date or boolean. A cell is `null` when unknown.
  - Money is an exact decimal string plus its own ISO currency. Numbers and percents are exact decimal strings too.
  - Totals are only typed SUM or AVERAGE over one column. They're refused over text or mixed currencies.
  - Each workbook carries its sources (record refs plus truth class) and a provenance line.
  - `artifact.ts:49` adds the type; `:626` the `workbook` field; `:944` the export formats `pdf|pptx|xlsx|csv`.
- **Renderer** (`packages/deck-render/src/spreadsheet.ts:256`, `:296`):
  - The .xlsx has a frozen header row and column widths, and is formatted by type (money in each cell's own currency, percent, date).
  - Totals are real formulas, unknown cells are blank, and the last sheet is "Sources".
  - The CSV is the first sheet only, with a byte-order mark so Excel reads accents, and a guard so text can't run as a formula.
  - `export.ts:49,69` routes spreadsheets to it.
- **Q tool** `make_spreadsheet` (`packages/q-tools/src/tools/spreadsheet.ts:207`; builders in `spreadsheet-build.ts`):
  - The reader picks the source by meaning: the pipeline, one company's stated figures, or a table, comparison or ranked list Q already showed in the conversation.
  - Code writes every cell. The model can only name the sheet and choose columns.
  - Company figures use `read_company_figures`' own permission check, so nothing new is exposed.
  - The spreadsheet is filed through the existing `fileOwnAnswer`. Its card appears on the answer through the same path `revise_my_document` uses.
  - It is not always on. Every always-on tool goes into every turn, and that set is already at the model's 128-tool limit. Instead it's offered on every purpose except ACTION_PREPARATION, and on any purpose when the reader names it.

  - The port (`composition/spreadsheets.ts`) reads Q's earlier answers as the run's owner. It's wired in at `main.ts:3580`.

- API: `createSituationAssembler({ tools, memory?, activity? }, options)` returns `{ assemble, research, invalidate }`.
  - `assemble({ context, subject, ask, journey?, publicProfile?, refresh? })` returns a `QSituationDossier`.
  - `research(dossier, { hook, ask, timeoutMs? })` adds the public-findings section.
- Every read goes through `QToolPort.execute` with the asker's own context, the same path chat tools use; nothing uses a service-role read. A founder dossier never calls investor tools and an investor dossier never calls founder-private ones. Labels the other side may not hold are dropped, and the contract checks again.

<result>I've built S4, S5 and S6 on `feat/plan-execution`, with tests using fake models and tools, and pushed after each commit. Two things to know first:
- **S4 and S5 are one commit, not two.** They share `main.ts` and `plans.ts`, so I couldn't split them cleanly.
- **Nothing is deployed or tried against a real database or real model.** The SQL, routes and card are covered only by in-memory fakes; the page was never driven in a browser.

Commits: `3dcd11a56` (S4+S5) and `9b2573570` (S6). Local HEAD equals `origin/feat/plan-execution` at `9b2573570`. No new migrations: everything uses lane A's three tables. Lane A/B contracts were changed only additively (listed under "Also changed in other lanes").

**S4 — the plan job** (`apps/q-api/src/composition/workforce/plan-job.ts`)
- `runPlanJob` (:919): gather the situation as the asker, then read the founder's deck in parallel with public research (research only when the reader asks for it), then draft, then two reviews in parallel, at most one redraft, then save the plan and version.
- If the plan still fails review it is offered as a draft, marked not fully reviewed, with its open points. If drafting fails, Q answers from what it already holds instead.
- Code, not the model, decides several things:
  - It drops citations that don't exist, and drops any step left with none (`groundPlan` :580).
  - It sets each step's owner and whether it needs approval from the action type (`classifyStep` :345).
  - It flags parts of the situation the plan ignored (`codeChecks` :702).
  - It maps lane B's 8-item review score onto the contract's 6-item rubric without changing the total (`reviewOf` :742).
- The "what you did recently" read is new (`activity.ts`): the person's own events, worded by code, one query.
- Plan jobs run on the existing durable queue (`runner.ts` `runPlan` :325) and the plan card is posted into the conversation (`delivery.ts` `announcePlan` :301). The progress card shows "usually 1–2 minutes" and "Gathering your situation" from the moment the job is queued.
- I added four plan stages to the live-progress contract and a plan-specific step bar on the work canvas, with Arabic.

**S5 — routing, the card and Execute**
- **Routing** (`answer.ts` :5876 and :5898): a plan of the person's own starts the job and replies at once. If the person names another company, it goes to the existing team job instead.
- **Keyword fast path deleted:** the `KINDS` regex and `workKindsAsked` are gone. Four existing tests that relied on it now set `teamJob: true` or a reply-to-Q reading instead.
- **Card and routes:** the plan card (`plan-card.tsx`) shows in chat, on the stage and on the Board. It is served by `GET /v1/q/plans/:planId` and `POST .../decide`, both added to the route-parity list.
- **Execute** (`plans.ts`):
  - Clicking it prepares one `q.plan.execute` approval card tied to the plan version, a hash of its content and its steps.
  - On approval, the person's steps become board tasks, with a reminder when dated.
  - Q's own research and document work starts directly.
  - Anything that goes out to another person gets its own approval card.
  - A changed plan makes the old approval do nothing.
- **"Change it"** files the person's words in the plan's thread and writes the next version, which needs Execute again.

**S6 — thread, direction, conditions, specialists**
- `plan-thread.ts` derives each step's state from append-only thread entries; only the status lines are ever shown to the person.
- **Direction:** the reader's `directsWork` saves the person's words once per turn. A plan still being written re-reads them before each draft. Jobs a plan started re-read them before every step (`withDirection`, `jobs.ts` :1054).

- **The team thread**: your messages while it runs are direction every step re-reads; any event in your account re-checks every open plan's waiting steps and fires the next ones; a step with no built-in role gets a named specialist, listed on the Team page.

### Claude — 2026-10-29 04:48 UTC

The planning live test on production found that planning isn't up to the bar yet. Only one of four runs reached the full flow, and no plan passed the 99/100 review. The test used fictional accounts only and cost about $0.16.

**What worked**
- The founder's "how do I improve my chances of getting investment?" produced a 9-step plan in about 80 seconds.
- The plan drew on Aster's interest, the deck gaps and the founder's readiness.
- "Change it" wrote a second version.
- Execute showed one approval card, and on approval Q started two of its steps as jobs.
- The pitch-deck and financial-documents ask started immediately without asking anything back. It showed live stages and quoted the deck's figures.

**What failed**
- **Board:** "Put on my board" reported success but created no board items. The board code hides the error and then says the tasks are "already there".
- **Plan-writing failures:** 7 of 19 plan-writing model calls returned output that failed validation. That broke the investor plan and both redrafts of the second version.
- **Reviews:** scores ranged from 65 to 91, so every plan was labelled a draft.
- **Wrong kind of answer:**
  - The investor's two-week plan and the hire-a-CFO request became research memos instead of plans.

### Claude — 2026-10-29 05:34 UTC

I started tracing the planning defects myself from production logs, the database and the code. None of the main failures were random model mistakes; each had a specific, fixable cause. The fixes are not done yet: the planning fix lane is applying them now, and it was resumed after a container restart stopped it.

**Why planning failed**
- **Board:** "Put on my board" silently placed nothing. The board table only accepts a standard unique ID for the key that stops duplicate tasks, and the plan code passed a text label instead. Postgres rejected every insert, and the code swallowed the error and said the tasks were "already there". The unit tests used a fake board, so they never caught it.
- **Rejected plans:** 7 of 19 plan writes came back as invalid output. The production logs show the exact reasons:
  - a step listed more than 5 "done when" items or more than 8 cited facts;
  - one step had an extra field.
  - One overflow threw away the entire plan, and the automatic retry sent the same prompt and failed the same way.
  - The same limits clipped the "why" text mid-word on almost every step. That is the "payback,…" text the tester saw.
- **Low review scores:** the writer and both "independent" reviewers all run on the same standard model, under the budget meant for simple data extraction. The reviewers' notes are fair: generic research steps, steps resting on unverified claims, and proposing to share a private report without the founder's approval. With only one redraft allowed, a draft scoring 65 to 85 has no path to 99.
- **Pitch-deck review became a plan:** the turn reader got it right and labelled it a document review. The code then sends every document review to the plan job, by design, with a hard-coded reply from an older version of the ask. That came from how the requirement was written down, not from the model.
- **Investor plans never happen:** naming any company sends the request away from planning by rule. That excludes almost every investor plan, because investors plan around named companies in their pipeline.

The fix lane has all of this, with directions:
- give each board task a stable unique ID and stop hiding board errors;
- trim overflowing lists instead of rejecting the whole plan;
- move planning to the stronger task class meant for reasoning;
- route each kind of ask to the right place;
- keep the 99 bar.

If it finds 99 can't be reached within six model calls on the models we have, it will report the numbers and I'll bring that choice to you.

**Two unsafe changes I removed from the stress fixes**
- A bare "yes" could approve a waiting card even when Q's last question was about something else. Q's "Want me to open it?" followed by "yes" would have approved the wrong action. I reverted that. The reader decides again, and Q's existing reminder tells the person the card is still waiting.
- Whether Q reads a company's data room depended on an English keyword list. A French or Arabic question would never trigger it. Now being on the company's page is the trigger, with the read size capped.

### Claude — 2026-10-29 07:43 UTC

Web search still isn't working after your renewal, and the new Serper key isn't being read at all. Your research spec was the right test: today's pipeline covers only part of it, so I've started building the rest.

**Search keys.** One search ran at 07:28, after q-api restarted with your changes:
- **Serper:** you added the new key as `RESERP_API` on q-api and workers. The code never reads that name. Rename it to `SERPER_API_KEY`, the name Q reads for serper.dev. `SERP_API_KEY` belongs to SerpApi, a different company.
- **Brave:** still returned 402 (payment required). The renewal probably sits on a different key or subscription from the one stored in Railway as `BRAVE_API`. Check that `BRAVE_API` holds the key from the renewed plan.
- **Tavily:** 432, credit used up.
- **ScrapingBee:** 401, key refused.

Q pauses a failing provider for 15 minutes before retrying it. So searches resume within 15 minutes of a correct key being in place, or straight away after a redeploy.

**How deep is the research today?** It does the core properly:
- a model plans 6 to 12 focused questions;
- they run in parallel across the search providers and the best pages are read;
- facts are extracted with dates and sources, and one with a number is kept only if that number appears on its page;
- a writer drafts the report and a critic reviews it.

Against your spec, these parts are missing or weak:
- **Iteration:** one follow-up round, then it stops.
- **Conflicting sources:** nothing detects them or shows both sides.
- **Stale sources:** nothing checks the dates.
- **Primary sources:** regulators, filings and registries get only a small ranking boost.
- **Capital Q's own companies:** companies on Capital Q in the sector aren't included, filtered by what the investor is allowed to see.
- **Durable state:** an investigation lost to a restart starts over.
- **Thesis implications:** no section tests the findings against the investor's thesis.
- **Limits of public search:** nothing says plainly what search cannot establish, such as private revenue, beneficial ownership or fund commitments.

On orchestration: Q doesn't use LangGraph, and we chose earlier not to add LangChain or LangGraph. The pipeline lives in Q's own orchestrator and job runner, so the new work goes there.

**What's being built now** extends the existing pipeline rather than adding a second one:
- **Iteration:** a bounded loop that keeps searching the open gaps until they close or the budget runs out.
- **Cross-checking in code:** facts confirmed by two independent sites are marked as such, disagreeing figures are kept side by side, and old ones are flagged stale.
- **Primary sources:** sources are ranked primary or secondary, and primary sources are searched for first.
- **Capital Q companies:** included only as far as the investor is allowed to see them.
- **Durable state:** progress is saved after every round, so a restart resumes rather than starting over.
- **Progress:** visible on the job card each round.
- **Report shape:** dated developments, regulatory risks, competitors, opportunities, implications for the investor's own thesis, contradictions, what public sources cannot establish, and next actions.

The lane is told never to seed or hard-code any example company or sector; tests use made-up data only. A live test of it needs working search keys first.

The planning batch deploys once its CI is green; the check runs at 07:45 UTC.

**What each part does**
1. **Bounded loop** (`apps/q-api/src/composition/workforce/deep-research.ts`): after each round, code finds the open gaps — a planned topic with no admitted fact or whose search could not run, facts that disagree, only out-of-date facts, or no official source where one is expected. The planner is asked for queries for those gaps only, and anything outside them is dropped. A planned search that never ran is re-sent as planned, with no model call. The loop stops on: no gaps, round cap, search budget, model budget, deadline, or nothing new to ask.
2. **Cross-source validation in code** (`packages/q-research/src/domain/cross-check.ts`):
   - Facts are grouped by the reader's measure/entity labels (or shared wording within a topic) and only compared within the same period and unit.
   - Figures within 5% from independent publishers become `MULTI_SOURCE_SUPPORTED`. Independence means a different registrable domain, and the same story under the same title on several sites counts once.
   - Disagreeing figures are both marked `CONTRADICTORY`, each naming the other, and both are kept.
   - Facts older than their topic's horizon are `STALE` (news 18 months, regulation 24, market data 36, other 60). Undated facts are never stale.
   - A company's own disclosure is `SELF_REPORTED`.
3. **Source tiers** (`domain/source-tier.ts`): primary means a government-style domain in any country, a small supranational set, an official body whose domain matches its own name, or a company's own disclosure (labelled as its claim). Secondary is accountable press and research houses; everything else is other. Ranking puts primary first, and the report shows the tier for each source.
4. **Capital Q records** (`capital-q-records.ts`, wired in `main.ts`): the existing company search tool runs as the person under their firewall plan. Results are kept apart from web facts and labelled for the writer. The planner never sees them and they never enter a query. The investor's mandate and pipeline still come in through the existing `own-context.ts`.
5. **Durable state** (`queue.ts`, `runner.ts`, `jobs.ts`, `ports.ts`): the investigation is saved on the job's existing row after each phase of each round. No migration was needed. A restart resumes and the job's search budget is not refilled. Page text is kept only until that round's facts are read.

7. **Report**: new prompt versions only (`RESEARCH_PLAN` v4, `RESEARCH_FACTS` v3, `ANALYSIS_WRITE` v5) and the prompt lock is regenerated. The model writes the eight requested sections. Code writes "Contradictions" (both sides, both cited), "What public sources cannot establish" (including which topics no provider could search), a tiered Sources list, and per-fact evidence and status.   - topics where no official source has been found.
- **It cross-checks in code, not by asking a model.**
  - Matching figures from different publishers count as corroborated. The same story copied across sites counts once.
  - Disagreeing figures are both kept and point at each other.
  - Old facts are marked stale: news after 18 months, regulation after 24, market data after 36.
- **It puts primary sources first.** Government and regulator sites in any country, official bodies, and company disclosures (labelled as the company's claim) come ahead of press and research houses. Every source shows its tier in the report.
- **It includes Capital Q's own companies.** Only those the investor is allowed to see, kept separate from web findings, and never used in a search query.
- **It survives restarts.** Progress is saved after each phase, and a restart resumes without re-sending finished searches.
- **Progress shows on the job card:** "Planning the investigation", "Round 2: checking 4 open questions", "Cross-checking sources".
- **The report's contents:**
  - written by the model: dated developments, regulatory risks, competitors, opportunities, and the implications for the investor's own thesis;
  - written by code: the contradictions with both sides, "what public sources cannot establish", and the sources by tier.

One change of my own: the search budget per job was only 8, which would have stopped the loop after its first round. I raised it to 40, the size of one full investigation. Jobs only spend what their questions need, typically 12 to 24 searches. At your prices a full run is about 40 Serper credits or roughly 20 cents of Brave, so your 2,500 Serper credits cover about 60 full investigations.

All testing used fake providers and invented data, so no credits were spent. Once it's deployed I'll run at most two or three real investigations to prove it.

### Claude — 2026-10-29 13:58 UTC

Deep research isn't good enough yet. Both live runs fell short, and the main cause is already fixed on a branch, not yet deployed.

**Investor run, 4/10.**
- **What worked:** the investigation itself. Two rounds, 21 searches each on Brave and Serper, 39 sources read, every claim cited. The report has its contradictions section and its "what public sources can't establish" section, and Capital Q records were labelled separately from web facts. Model cost was about 5 cents and it took 3½ minutes.
- **What failed:** the content was almost all global. The filter that keeps private facts out of web searches only allows the person's own words. The person typed "Nigerian", so the planner's "Nigeria" and "CBN" were stripped from every query. Searches went out as plain "payments regulation", and the IRS, US Social Security and Singapore's regulator came back as "primary regulators".
- **The fix, which I made myself:** if the person names a country in any form, its other forms, such as "Nigeria" and "Lagos", may now leave too. Generic regulation words such as "central bank" and "circular" are also allowed. Private figures and countries the person never named still never leave. Tests prove both, and all 272 research tests pass.

**Founder run, 2/10.** It never became an investigation. Q's reading of the message timed out twice, and the request quietly fell back to a two-search chat answer, with no progress card and no document.

**Now in a fix lane**, each to be traced to its cause first:
- The investor's actual mandate wasn't seen, so the thesis section said "not recorded".
- Any government site counted as a primary source, and trade press was labelled a company disclosure.
- When Q can't read a message, it must not silently downgrade a research request.
- The new progress stages never showed on the card.
- Two figures were cited to a page that doesn't contain them.
- Evidence labels were inconsistent.

The cited sources I could check were real; four of five loaded, and the fifth blocked our fetch. The firewall held: no private figure or name appeared in any query.

The earlier fix batch is deploying now, covering the live plan card, the open-question resume and one count for Work. Once the research fixes land, I'll deploy them and run the two investigations again.

You're right on both counts, and the disappointment is fair.

**On context.** My fix only handled a country typed in words, which is too literal. Here is what research uses as context today:
- **Founders:** their own company's country and sectors already reach the search filter. The founder's run failed for a different reason: Q timed out reading the message, so research never started.
- **Investors:** nothing. Their declared mandate places (Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya) never reach the searches. A state or city such as Kano or Lagos State also doesn't bring its country along.

The research fix lane now has this as its top item:
- **States, regions and cities resolve to their country:** Nigeria's states, Kenya's counties, Ghana's regions and South Africa's provinces, held as reference data.
- **Earlier messages count:** places named earlier in the same conversation are included.
- **The investor's mandate counts:** their declared places and sectors are used, never cheque sizes or company names.
- **The planner is told the market explicitly:** "Nigeria, from your mandate". A question with no place anywhere stays global and the report says so.

**On the cycle.** There's no honest guarantee that a change never breaks anything. What I can change is how we prove the work before you see it. The 4/10 and 2/10 happened because the research code was only ever tested against made-up data. No real question went through the real search filter before release, so nobody noticed the filter stripping the country. That was my process failure, and the gate is being built now:
1. **Real cases, recorded once.** The two questions that failed, plus three more: a mandate-only investor, a "Lagos State" question, and a question with no place. Each is run once against real search, and the pages and model replies are saved. That costs about 40 searches per case, once.
2. **Replayed on every change, for free.** CI re-runs those cases with no network. Code checks each one:
   - every query carries the right country;
   - no private figure or name leaves;
   - primary sources come from the right country;
   - the report includes every required section and the investor's actual mandate;
   - every cited number is on its cited page.

   Any change that breaks one fails CI before deploy.
3. **Every live failure becomes a new case.** A mistake fixed once stays fixed, because its case runs forever after.

Deep research won't go back to you until it passes those cases. Then one live run will confirm it on production.

if we can get all this done, in your own opinion, Q is okay as an mvp then, right?

### Claude — 2026-10-29 15:51 UTC

Yes, with that list done, Q is a credible MVP. It already does things a plain chatbot can't: it works from the person's own account data, keeps private data private, plans and acts with approval, and produces real documents and spreadsheets. Finishing those items gets the core loop to the bar you've been holding.

Three things separate "a good demo" from "an MVP real people can rely on", and none of them are on that list:

1. **Real content in Discover.** The feed only shows companies with a playable pitch, so it's only as good as its pitches. Today it's mostly seeded demo companies. Five well-fitting telehealth companies were invisible this week for exactly that reason. An investor's first impression needs real founders with real pitches.
2. **Holding up with more than a few people at once.** The $100K estimate named two limits:
   - ranking makes about 360 database calls per request;
   - live voice calls are held in one server's memory, so a restart drops them.

   There are also no alerts. Today I find problems by running checks, not because something pages me. A handful of testers won't hit these limits, but a real launch will.
3. **Steady provider accounts.** Search, OpenAI and video all run on small prepaid balances. Tavily and ScrapingBee are already empty. One empty account quietly degrades Q, and users can't tell why.

There's also a smaller one: before inviting real customers, publish privacy terms that match what Q does with confidential documents.

My recommendation: finish the list, then invite a small closed group of real founders and investors, say 10 to 20, with you watching. That surfaces what tests can't, at a scale the current setup handles. Do the scaling work, alerts and provider top-ups before opening it wider.

**What was built**
1. **Settings → Security** (`/settings/security`, plus a new "Security" section on the Settings page): turning it on enrolls an authenticator app, shows the QR code and a copyable secret, then asks for the first code. The page shows whether it is on. Turning it off asks for a new code from the app before removing the factor, so an open session alone can't do it. Abandoned unfinished setups are cleaned up before a new one starts. The page uses the existing account layout and design tokens, and the new strings have Arabic entries (ui-text source regenerated).
2. **`/auth/two-step` page:** password sign-in, magic link, Google and recovery all route here when the user has a verified factor and the session is aal1. The safe `next` path is kept; recovery returns to `/auth/update-password`. The page has a "contact support" line for a lost device and a "Sign in as someone else" option.
3. **Unconfirmed email:** a password sign-in from an unconfirmed address shows "Confirm your email…" and a "Send the confirmation link again" button (`supabase.auth.resend`, then check-email). Supabase checks the password before confirmation status, so only someone with the right password sees this; a wrong password still gets the generic message.

**Where enforcement lives, and why**
- **api and q-api** (`packages/security`):
  - On the normal path, the existing session check on `auth.sessions` now also requires an aal2 token when the user has a verified row in `auth.mfa_factors`. I used the services' existing privileged DB connection rather than a RESTRICTIVE RLS policy: authentication runs before any RLS-scoped transaction, so refusing there covers every route, while a policy would have to be repeated on every table.
  - On the fallback path (Auth server), the factor list comes from the Auth server's answer and the level comes from the token it just accepted.
  - A missing or unexpected `aal` claim counts as aal1. The 15-second cache is keyed by assurance level, so a cached aal2 result never serves an aal1 token.
- **Web:** the session proxy sends an aal1 session that owes its code from every protected route to `/auth/two-step`. `getSessionUser` returns null for that session and `requireSessionUser` redirects it. Whether a factor exists comes from the Auth server (cached 60 seconds per user, cleared on turn-on/off), never from the session cookie, which the browser could edit. If the Auth server can't be reached, the user goes to the code page, which lets an un-enrolled user straight through.

- Package build (`turbo run build --filter=./packages/*`): 54/54 succeeded.
- Targeted vitest: 15 files, 324 tests passed. This covers `packages/security`, api and q-api authentication, the new `apps/web/test/auth-two-step.test.ts` (21 tests), route policy, landing proxy, Google auth, auth errors, i18n catalogue coverage, route-capability parity and registration journey.

With the welcome from the live defect, Talk to Q now sits above the composer at 1440×900. When a welcome is too tall to fit even with Q at its smallest, Talk to Q is still below the fold at rest and you reach it by scrolling.

**Root cause:** this was not a stacking problem. Q's resting room was a fixed square (`--cq-room-box`, 360px on desktop). Any welcome taller than the space left pushed the arrival column past the bottom of the scroll area. The scroll area clips at the composer's top edge, so Talk to Q (y 839–1102 locally, 842 live) was cut off there and looked as if it were under the composer. The earlier patch only shrank Q when the welcome held the weekly briefing.

**Change:**
- **`apps/web/app/globals.css`:** Q's room is now the arrival's one flexible item. It starts from zero, grows up to its full size and never goes below a third of it. So the welcome gets its height first and Q takes what is left. If even the smallest Q doesn't fit, the arrival grows (`min-h-full` stays) and the area scrolls to Talk to Q. I removed the briefing-only `:has()` rule.
- **`apps/web/src/features/briefing/arrival-room.tsx`:** while the room is empty and not wide, its wrapper boxes are `display: contents`. That makes Q's room a direct child of the arrival column. The side columns stay mounted for the stage's cards but are hidden until the room fills.
- **`apps/web/src/features/q/q-conversation.tsx`:** a ResizeObserver (`fitRoomPresence`) scales Q's drawing to the box it was given. The scale goes into the existing transform, so Q stays centred at rest and when gathered. There is no new z-index, colours use tokens only, and reduced motion still turns the transition off. Phone layout is unchanged because the room is already hidden below 1024px.
- **Tests:** added `apps/web/test/home-fold.test.tsx` (CSS contract plus a rendered check of the room's wrappers) and removed the old briefing-only block from `e11-panel-swipe-and-live-question.test.ts`.

**Proof:** I ran the web app locally (`next dev` against production's public endpoints, fictional accounts) and made the welcome variants by adding content to the page. Variant d is the live defect exactly as production serves it.

| b (+ weekly briefing cards), c (+ Finish setup + returning cards) | Q at its smallest, still too tall; reachable by scrolling | same |
